newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine coconut exports seen rising in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Philippine coconut exports seen rising in 1997.

text.p: Philippine coconut exports are expected to rise next year as local harvests recover from typhoon damage, the United Coconut Associations of the Philippines Inc (UCAP) said on Tuesday.

The coconut crop in the Philippines, the world's largest exporter of coconut products, is expected to rise by 8.9 percent to 2.142 million tonnes in copra terms in 1997 from this year's forecast 1.966 million tonnes, the trade group said.
"For 1997, it is projected that production is to slightly recover owing to this year's good precipitation levels," UCAP said in a report.
UCAP lowered its crop forecast for this year to 1.966 million tonnes from an earlier 2.334 million.

"The very low export turnout since the start of the year has only demonstrated that the twin effects of last year's typhoon damage and stressed trees undergoing recovery from heavy fruiting have been more severe than anticipated," it said.
Coconut exports in copra terms in 1997 were forecast to reach 1.536 million tonnes, the bulk of which would be coconut oil, it said.
The group said it expected coconut exports to fall to 1.426 million tonnes this year from the year-ago 2.265 million tonnes.
Exports of coconut oil alone are seen reaching 900,000 tonnes in 1997, up from this year's forecast of 840,000 tonnes, but down from 1995's 1.34 million tonnes.

"Gauging from the rainfall pattern this year, it is anticipated that export volumes during the first semester next year would be bigger, representing 53 percent of the annual total, compared to the second semester tonnage," UCAP said.
Manila vegetable oil traders said the UCAP export forecasts were within their expectations.
"But I don't agree with their projection that exports would be stronger in the first half of 1997 compared to the second half," said one trader in one of the country's largest oil mills.
Another trader said current copra harvests from coconut plantations on the southern island of Mindanao were not as abundant as expected.
"The UCAP projection of a 150,000 tonnes inventory at the end of this year is not enough to push exports significantly higher in early 1997," the trader added.

UCAP said it expected the country's export receipts from coconut oil to rise by 6.3 percent to $660.6 million in 1997 from a projected $621.5 million this year, due to expectations of lower supply of other vegetable oils next year.
"Early indications from other seed oils point to lower availability at that time which should generally reflect better price levels for vegetable oils, including coconut oil," UCAP said.
